sections.text: A program is a list of instructions for a computer. The computer follows them exactly, one after another, from top to bottom, unless an instruction tells it to jump somewhere else (you'll see how in the next lessons).
Computers are fast but very literal. They do what you wrote, not what you meant. That's why programming languages have strict rules: a missing symbol can stop the whole program.
Here is a complete Rust program. Don't worry about every symbol yet. Look at the three lines inside the curly braces:
Each println! line shows one line of text. Because the computer goes top to bottom, the three messages always appear in this order.

Before a Rust program runs, a tool called the compiler translates it into instructions the computer can run. While doing that it checks for mistakes. If it finds one, it explains the problem instead of producing a program. Compiler errors are normal and helpful, not a sign you're doing badly.

exercise.prompt: Swap the lines so the program prints First, then Second, each on its own line.
hints: The computer runs your lines from top to bottom. Which line should run first?
Each println! line is one whole instruction ending with ;. Move println!("First"); above println!("Second");, still inside the curly braces.

quiz.question: In what order does a computer run the lines inside main, when nothing tells it to jump?
What does the compiler do?
options: Turns your code into a runnable program, checking it for mistakes first
Saves your code to a file and keeps a backup copy of it
Writes the program for you from a plain-English description
